episodes.157244: There were several low-topped supercells that developed along a warm front across Southern Minnesota Wednesday evening, May 19, 2021. These storms produced 7 short-lived tornadoes and several funnel clouds across southern Minnesota. These tornadoes were weak and most rated EF0. This was a marginal CAPE, marginal wind shear environment with low cloud bases. A strengthening low-level jet led to an increase in low-level wind shear. This was able to produce a few low-topped supercells that were efficient tornado producers.
episodes.157454: A thunderstorm produced penny sized hail near Fairpoint as it moved northwest across northern Meade County.
episodes.157577: A deep longwave trough remained anchored over the Central and Southern Rockies on May 20th, with a deep southerly fetch of low level moisture continuing to maintain an ample moisture-rich environment over the Four State Region. Diurnal heating contributed to air mass destabilization during the afternoon, with disturbances aloft contributing to scattered shower and isolated thunderstorm development across the area. Low level shear increased during the afternoon, and helped foster the development of isolated severe thunderstorms across portions of East Texas, with isolated tornadoes briefly touching down across Western Angelina and Western Harrison Counties. A localized pocket of damaging winds also resulted in large limbs being downed near Lufkin, and a porch being damaged as well. These storms eventually shifted north into Southeast Oklahoma during the evening.
episodes.157691: Some residual storms associated with a slow moving upper level low pressure system that generated severe storms the days prior, continued to move across the eastern Texas Panhandle on the 19th. Most of these storms just brought some good rainfall to the area as instability was limited but one them did produce a wind gust of 58 mph as a heavy rainfall and downdraft occurred over the mesonet site located near Wellington, Texas.
episodes.157764: Widespread heavy rainfall across the Neches River basin in East Texas throughout much of May resulted in moderate flooding along the Neches River near Alto.
episodes.157812: A thunderstorm moved northward over Johnson County, Wyoming. The public reported penny size hail east of Buffalo, Wyoming.
episodes.158284: Isolated dryline thunderstorms developed on the evening of May 16, well in advance of an approaching upper level low.  These storms produced an EF-0 tornado on the north side of Anson, and large hail and damaging winds in Fisher and Haskell Counties.  An approaching upper low from New Mexico interacted with a warm front on May 17, and produced a long track EF2 tornado across northern Sterling County along with several severe weather reports.  Many storm chasers videotaped this tornado as it tracked across the wind farms.  Heavy rain resulted in some flash flooding in Fisher County on the night of May 18 and in Irion County on the afternoon of May 19.
episodes.158656: A short-lived small, swirling wind, likely a gustnado, was captured on video. It did minor damage to an apartment building.
episodes.158710: An upper level trough was located over eastern New Mexico with a very dry atmosphere in place over south-central New Mexico.  Just enough instability existed for some isolated thunderstorms to develop and produce some damaging winds around Boles Acres.
episodes.158767: Within an area of scattered convection an isolated weak tornado formed and damaged power lines and power poles within a narrow south to north path on two west-east roads about a mile apart.
episodes.158887: In the late evening hours on May 19th, 2021, a small cluster of thunderstorms developed in a moist, unstable environment drifting towards the northwest. One embedded supercell developed a brief, weak tornado.
episodes.158888: On May 20th, 2021 a slow moving squall line and cluster of thunderstorms associated with a weak mid-level disturbance delivered torrential rainfall to portions of southeastern Louisiana, resulting in areas of flash flooding.
episodes.158889: Early on May 20th, 2021 a slow moving squall line and cluster of thunderstorms associated with a weak mid-level disturbance delivered severe wind gusts across marine areas.
episodes.159027: Heavy rain brought flooding to the Ouachita and Fourche LaFave Rivers in the middle of May.
episodes.159166: Scattered severe thunderstorms brought strong winds, wind damage, and hail to northern Utah.
episodes.159275: Isolated gale-force wind gusts in association with convective showers occurred west of Key West and offshore Marathon.  A strong easterly lower tropospheric flow was present; south of a strong subtropical ridge of high pressure.

events.narrative: The public reported some wind damage south of Boles Acres which was likely the result of a microburst or gustnado.

A storm chaser took video of a brief funnel cloud. It might have made ground contact but it was not possible to tell from the video, nor was there any damage noted. Therefore this has been recorded as a funnel cloud.

Numerous videos, including some from trained spotters, showed a funnel cloud west of Owatonna. Toward the end, it became rope-like and then dissipated. None of the videos were close-up, and no debris cloud was ever noted, so ground contact contact could not be confirmed by video.  Two surveys by local officials and the NWS revealed no damage anywhere. Therefore this has been recorded as a funnel cloud. Videos showed another funnel cloud close to this one, and a separate entry has been made for that funnel.

The Irion County Sheriff's Office reported numerous locations along FM 163 north of Barnhart under water with debris floating in the roadway.  Flooding was also reported on CR 401 and CR 131.

Two different trained spotters took video of a tornado that made ground contact in far northern Steele County, where about a dozen trees were broken per a NWS damage survey. It tracked north and moved into Rice County. One of the videos showed this tornado was the larger tornado, with another narrow tornado to its east that had characteristics similar to that of a satellite tornado.

A trained spotter took video of a brief tornado that touched down in a wooded area and knocked down large branches.  Another spotter was also monitoring the storm. The tornado was also caught on video by a MNDOT camera along I-35 near Clinton Falls, so the timing could be confirmed. A broader view of the storm suggested this tornado had some characteristics similar to that of a satellite tornado just east of a larger tornado.

Trained spotters took video of a tornado that touched down in an open field and moved northward. It struck a farmstead at the end of its path, with only large branches knocked down per a NWS damage survey.

A tornado touched town along East Heather Drive near Elderberry Drive and damaged a fence line along East Heather.  The tornado continued west crossing Texaco Road where an apartment complex had some damage to a few buildings consisting mostly of vinyl siding that was removed. The tornado then continued into the subdivision crossing St. John Street, where a residence had roof damage and St. Anthony Street where some tree damage was noted. The tornado reached max intensity as it crossed Wanda Street and Mimosa Avenue where it did damage to a patio cover and trees and removed the roof panels off of a shed in the backyard of a home on Wade Street. One of the roof panels to the shed was carried approximately 125 yards to the south where it landed on a home on Mimosa Avenue. The tornado appears to have lifted near the 300 block of Wade Street.

A brief touchdown was reported east-northeast of Henderson as it crossed Highway 19, moving from Le Sueur County into Scott County. It blew a trampoline and damaged a play set on the Le Sueur County side before moving north and damaging some trees in a grove  in Scott County per a NWS damage survey.

Widespread rainfall amounts of fifteen to in excess of twenty inches fell across the Neches River basin of East Texas during May. As a result, the Neches River southwest of Alto near Highway 21 rose above the 16 foot flood stage at 1030 pm on May 9th, reached the 18 foot moderate flood stage at 9 pm on the 19th, before cresting at 19.2 feet at 9 am on the 24th. A slow recession commenced afterwards, with the Neches River falling to near 17.7 feet by midnight on the 31st. Additional heavy rainfall moved into the Neches River basin late in the day on the 31st, which resulted in a sharp and significant secondary crest above the 20 foot major flood stage on June 1st. ||This flooding resulted in moderate to severe flooding of the heavily wooded floodplain, with boat ramps and picnic areas completely inundated.
The Salt Flat sensor recorded a peak wind gust of 63 mph.

An EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 100 mph touched down on the south end of a large property along Old Bonner Road and tracked north-northwest for at least an estimated 2.5 miles through rural areas of Northwest Angelina County. Much of the damage was observed in this large property area, with damage mainly confined to numerous trees being uprooted, trunks snapped, or losing large branches. One outbuilding did receive minor damage on the outskirts of the tornado on this property. The tornadic damage extended as far as the eye could see south of the south boundary of the aforementioned property, although access to survey farther south was unavailable due to a lack of road access. The tornado continued north across Blackburn Switch Road, where a narrow swath of EF-0 tree damage was observed. This was judged to be the ending point of this tornado due to the lack of access to roads farther north, just south of Highway 103.
A porch attached to a home was damaged. Large limbs were also downed as well near the home.

Reliable drone footage shared through social media documented a very brief touchdown of a small tornado on a pond north of Hallsville. The vortex dissipated while encountering a tree line just north of the pond and no tree damage was observed in the high resolution footage. Due to no damage indicators, this tornado will be classified as an EF-Unknown.
The public reported penny size hail in eastern Johnson County, Wyoming.

Emergency management from DeKalb County notified the office that there were power poles and power lines down on two roads that are about a mile apart. The path of damage between these two roads was pretty narrow, and radar indicated some weak rotation, so a tornado was deemed the reason for the damage.
